reviews.review:
ArcRunner is a highly polished, vibrantly coloured third-person roguelike shooter with cooperative play set in a futuristic cyberpunk world. At first blush, it's a game that should be directly up my alley--so, why the Negative review?

Well, despite all the flash and polish, ArcRunner ends up feeling stale, repetitive and uninspired. This largely comes down to upgrades that don't feel like they significantly alter your playstyle in any way combined with the game's three classes playing very similarly to begin with. Additionally, while the game does feature a wide suite of unlockable weaponry, these too fail to distinguish themselves, and you'll likely find yourself falling back on the same (quickly unlocked) Assault Rifle/Shotgun setup time and time again.

So how does ArcRunner improve? First of all, pull the camera back so you can do more creative things with your class abilities without cluttering the screen. Next, get wild with your weaponry; it's a cyberpunk world, and the only (arguably) creative weapons are a disc thrower and a lightning gun. Hardly pushing the boundaries there. Look for additional inspiration when crafting your rooms, and if you're going to have several upgrades that improve vertical mobility, ADD VERTICAL ELEMENTS TO YOUR LEVELS. Your player shouldn't always end up walking along the outer wall of a warehouse shooting at the enemies that all spawn within easy each.

Speaking of upgrades, each one should ideally make a meaningful impact on how your players' experience, empowering their fantasy of being futuristic super cyborgs. Instead, these were far and away the most "useful" upgrades in ArcRunner:

- Sprint 50% faster for 2 seconds when you begin running.
- Range and critical chance increase incrementally.
- Reload speed increases incrementally.
- Defensive shoulder weapon that periodically fires at nearby enemies.

These should all (with the possible exception of the shoulder weapon) be bonus upgrades that come with the thing you actually want. None of them are exciting enough to be their own upgrade.

Roguelikes are ultimately about players chasing (and occasionally catching!) that "overpowered" state where they feel like they have cheated somehow or broken the game--unfortunately, with ArcRunner's staid design philosophy, that fantasy just isn't possible.

Any comparisons to Risk of Rain 2 are only skindeep; don't be taken in by them.

It's a fun rogue-like shooter with fairly simple progression.

I like the classes, I just wish thete were more!

This reminds me of Global Agenda to a degree.
